title: Sound Lab 1: ship vs sheep, question melody
objective: Hear and produce short i vs long ee, and rising vs falling question melody.
intro_md:
[L1: English has two different vowel sounds that many languages write the same way: the short, quick i in "this" and "six", and the long ee in "see" and "three". Whole words change meaning with this one sound — like "ship" (a boat) and "sheep" (the animal). Today you train your ear with words you already know. You also train question melody: yes/no questions go UP at the end; questions with What and Where go DOWN. The melody tells your listener what kind of answer you want.]
{{l1_contrast:vowel_short_i_vs_long_ee}}
notes: TODO_audio: every exercise in this lesson needs recorded audio (1, 2 as model audio per word, 3, 4, 5, 9 as quoted prompts); written prompts stand in for the recordings. Exercises 7-8 need ASR with pitch-contour scoring. No new vocabulary by design (band map allocates 0 to L16); all material recycles taught words.

exercises.prompt: [audio, 0.75x] 'this' … 'these' — [L1: Are the two words the same or different?]
exercises.rationale: AX same/different discrimination is the entry task of perception-first pronunciation work; this/these is a real minimal pair built from words the learner already reads.

options.label: [L1: different]
options.rationale: 'this' has the short i, 'these' has the long ee — one sound, two words.

options.label: [L1: the same]
options.rationale: If they sounded the same, the vowel length difference is not registering yet — replay at 0.75x.

exercises.prompt: [L1: Listen to each word. Put it in the short-i group or the long-ee group.]
exercises.rationale: Categorizing known words by vowel builds the two sound boxes before new contrasts arrive; es has only one tense /i/, so the short lax i does not exist for es speakers — sorting makes it audible.

exercises.prompt: [audio, 0.75x] 'fifteen' — [L1: Which part of the word is long?]
exercises.rationale: One word containing BOTH target sounds; hearing fif- (short) vs -teen (long) also prepares the fifteen/fifty distinction that phone numbers (L11) depend on.

options.label: [L1: the end: -teen]
options.rationale: -teen has the long ee — that length is why -teen numbers are easy to hear.

options.label: [L1: the start: fif-]
options.rationale: fif- has the short, quick i — if it sounded long, the two boxes are swapped.

exercises.prompt: [audio, 1.0x] 'Are you from Mexico?' — [L1: Does the voice go UP or DOWN at the end?]
exercises.rationale: Yes/no melody made explicit after L09 met it implicitly; melody signals question type before the words are parsed (pron target P3).

options.label: [L1: UP]
options.rationale: Yes/no questions rise at the end — the rise says: answer yes or no.

options.label: [L1: DOWN]
options.rationale: Falling melody belongs to What/Where questions and statements.

exercises.prompt: [audio, 1.0x] 'Where are you from?' — [L1: Does the voice go UP or DOWN at the end?]
exercises.rationale: Minimal melody contrast with the previous item; es and zh speakers often rise on ALL questions, so the WH-fall is the trained direction.

options.label: [L1: DOWN]
options.rationale: What/Where questions fall — the question word already marks the question.

options.label: [L1: UP]
options.rationale: Rising every question is the predicted transfer habit — WH-questions fall.

exercises.prompt: [L1: UP or DOWN? Match each question to its melody.]
exercises.rationale: Applies the rise/fall rule across the unit's four real questions — the same four the learner must produce in the L17 dialogue.

exercises.prompt: [L1: Ask this question out loud. Make your voice go UP at the end:] Are you from Mexico?
asr_focus: rising final contour on the last word
exercises.rationale: Production only after perception (perception-first rule); the words are all known, so all attention goes to the rising contour.

exercises.prompt: [L1: Now ask this question with your voice going DOWN at the end:] Where are you from?
exercises.rationale: Contrast pair with the previous item: same voice, opposite contour — the down-melody is the counter-habit move for learners who rise on every question.
The unit's clearest minimal melody pair: rising Sorry? (repair, L15) vs falling I'm sorry (apology) — melody alone decides the meaning.

options.label: [L1: UP — say it again, please]
options.rationale: Rising Sorry? asks for repetition, exactly as taught in L15.

options.label: [L1: DOWN — I apologize]
options.rationale: The falling version is the apology 'I'm sorry.' — a different move.
